`quarto-simulator` is a Quarto extension for **teaching the basics of Quarto
and markdown inside a Quarto lesson**. It turns a block in the lesson into an
editor and a live preview that *simulate* `quarto render`, with optional
graded exercises. Everything runs in the learner's browser: there is nothing
to install and no server to run.

Try it. Change the text on the left, then press **▶ Render** (or
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>K</kbd>):

````{quarto-simulator}
#| height: 420
---
title: "Hello, Quarto"
author: "Your name"
toc: true
---

## Markdown

Quarto documents are written in **markdown**: *italics*, `code`,
[links](https://quarto.org) and lists.

- One
- Two

## Callouts

::: {.callout-tip}
Callouts, cross-references and tables of contents are rendered by
Quarto's own Lua filters, so they look the way they do in real Quarto.
:::

| Tool   | Role                       |
|--------|----------------------------|
| pandoc | Converts markdown to HTML  |
| Quarto | Adds everything else       |
````

::: {.callout-important}
## A simulation, not Quarto
The markdown-to-HTML step is real: Quarto 1.10's own reader, Lua filters and
template run in a WebAssembly build of pandoc. The rest is reimplemented for
the browser: reading the YAML, running R (webR) and Python (Pyodide), and
part of Quarto's HTML post-processing. Only HTML output is supported.
[How it works](vignettes/how-it-works.qmd) has the details.
:::

## Install

```bash
quarto add ryjohnson09/quarto-simulator
```

Then add the filter to a lesson and write a `quarto-simulator` block, with
more backticks than any fence inside it:

`````markdown
---
title: "My lesson"
engine: markdown
filters:
  - quarto-simulator
---

````{quarto-simulator}
---
title: "Hello"
---

Some **markdown** to start from.
````
`````

`engine: markdown` stops knitr or Jupyter from running the code cells inside
playgrounds when the lesson itself renders.

## What it can do

- **Real Quarto output.** Callouts, cross-references, figures, tabsets,
  equations and the table of contents come from Quarto's own filters.
- **R and Python.** R cells run in webR and Python cells in Pyodide, with
  plots, tables, cell options and inline code.
- **Exercises.** Hints, solutions and checks written in a few lines of
  JavaScript, with feedback in the learner's words.
- **Helpful errors.** YAML mistakes point to the line, unknown options get
  "did you mean" suggestions, and failed cells say which cell failed.
- **A familiar editor.** Syntax highlighting modelled on Positron, shaded code
  cells and the RStudio render shortcut. Edits are saved in the browser.
